article_title: Too Good for Drugs (TGFD) (Character Education)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Too Good for Drugs. https://www.mendezfoundation.org
title: Skill-building lesson pattern combining cooperative learning, role-play, and application across contexts for social and resistance skills
description: The program's lesson design pattern pairs explicit instruction in named skills with active practice formats: "Instructional strategies cover goal setting and decisionmaking skills, prosocial skills, resistance to negative peer influence skills, and interpersonal skills." Within each scripted lesson, "Cooperative learning activities, role-play, and skill-building methods reinforce positive behaviors and skills and encourage students to apply these behaviors and skills in other contexts." The pattern embeds character values (respect for self and others, empathic responding, responsibility) into most lessons rather than teaching them separately, and lessons include information about drug use frequency and harmful effects.
requirements: Scripted lessons delivered by trained teachers or program instructors
Grade-level kits including student workbooks and lesson extenders
constraints: Evaluated as a classroom-based (not schoolwide) intervention in the reviewed studies
target_learners: Elementary school students
Middle school students
target_learning_goals: Prosocial skills
Resistance to negative peer influence
Goal setting and decisionmaking
Interpersonal skills
examples: Students engaged in role-play and cooperative learning games and were encouraged to apply the skills to different contexts across the 10 scripted lessons at each grade level
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Too Good for Drugs. https://www.mendezfoundation.org

article_title: Finding root causes effectively: A powerful way to improve schools
citation: Andrew Hegedus. (2010). Finding root causes effectively: A powerful way to improve schools. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Improve SIP quality through better determination of root causes so staff efforts are focused on improving results
description: The paper recommends improving School Improvement Plan quality by determining root causes more effectively, because plans that address symptoms are unlikely to improve achievement. As printed, improving SIP quality through better root-cause determination means "staff and administrative efforts will be more focused and directed in ways that have a higher likelihood of improving results." The recommendations also support developing a collaborative, inquiry-based culture.
requirements: School teams must determine root causes rather than surface symptoms when building improvement plans
constraints: NCLB-mandated consequences increase pressure to address root causes but do not themselves help schools determine or remove them
target_learners: school staff and administrators
target_learning_goals: focused school improvement efforts with a higher likelihood of improving student results
examples: The paper provides proposals for the entire SIP process and for school district central office support based on lessons learned developing the recommended process, protocols and tools
key_sources: Andrew Hegedus. (2010). Finding root causes effectively: A powerful way to improve schools. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/finding-root-causes-effectively-a-powerful-way-to-improve-schools/

article_title: Missing More than School: Reducing Chronic Absence for American Indian and Alaska Native Students
citation: Chang, H.N., & Leong, C. (2024). Missing more than school: Reducing chronic absence for American Indian and Alaska Native students. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Four-category taxonomy of root causes of chronic absenteeism: barriers, aversion, disengagement, and misconceptions
description: The brief organizes the reasons students miss school into four categories. As printed, "Figure 3 groups the reasons for absenteeism into four categories: barriers, aversion, disengagement, and misconceptions." Barriers include chronic illness, limited transportation, and housing and food insecurity; aversion includes unwelcoming school climate, anxiety, and biased disciplinary practices; disengagement includes boredom and lack of meaningful relationships with adults; misconceptions include beliefs that absences are only problematic if unexcused. The brief uses this taxonomy to argue that when large numbers of students are affected, systemic challenges beyond a student's or family's control are indicated.
requirements: Understanding the underlying causes of chronic absenteeism is treated as essential for devising effective solutions to improve attendance
constraints: The brief states these causes reflect systemic challenges in the community and in schools beyond a student's or family's control when large numbers of students are affected
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly American Indian/Alaska Native students
target_learning_goals: Regular school attendance and engagement in learning
examples: The brief maps issues commonly affecting AI/AN students' attendance, such as higher prevalence of chronic illness and limited health care access, onto these four categories
key_sources: Chang, H.N., & Leong, C. (2024). Missing more than school: Reducing chronic absence for American Indian and Alaska Native students. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655926

article_title: Educators Collaborating to Improve Mathematics: Three Structures That Mattered in Math in Common Districts
citation: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Educators collaborating to improve mathematics: Three structures that mattered in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/permissions
title: Role-diverse sense-making teams that interpret standards and carry a consistent districtwide message
description: This pattern brings together staff from many roles — teachers, coaches, principals, math department staff, and district administrators — to interpret standards, create implementation visions, and promote them systemwide. The report states these teams "can interpret and make sense of standards, create visions for the standards implementation in the real contexts of the district and its classrooms, and then protect and promote these visions throughout the system." Teams functioned as PLCs or task-focused groups working on instructional materials, observation tools, or parent education.
requirements: Teams must be a diverse and complementary mix of system leaders and educators representing varying roles, perspectives, and expertise from across the district
Collaboration must be intentionally centered on shifting a particular facet of the dynamics of classroom instruction or a specific monitoring structure
constraints: The report notes districts experienced repeated leadership turnover; participating staff served as keepers of the vision amid organizational turmoil
target_learners: District administrators, principals, coaches, and teachers implementing new standards
target_learning_goals: Developing shared understanding of standards and consistent messaging about standards-aligned instruction
examples: Dinuba Unified developed a classroom observation rubric and protocol through a role-diverse team, recalibrating as principals and coaches joined
Oakland used a site-based mini-grant program to incentivize role-diverse teams to write standards-implementation plans

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Build robust systems across school domains to prepare for and contain distress before it spreads
description: The report's first finding is that well-articulated and implemented systems running through key school processes prepare schools to overcome stressors. Systems act as "a backbone and intentionality to the school's operations, reducing confusion, unknowns, and opportunities for issues to go unaddressed and spiral into deeper decline." Robust systems buffer a stressor in one area so it does not spread to other domains; as the report puts it, "Stabilizing one domain allows you to stabilize others, isolating the spiral of distress to one area of the school."
requirements: Key systems in each core domain, including enrollment maintenance, leader and teacher development, consistent disciplinary processes, curricular alignment, and effective student support
constraints: Without systems, schools operate in crisis mode and institutional knowledge disappears when leaders leave; network-level systems inhibited school leaders when distant networks ignored local context
target_learners: Charter school leaders
Governing board members
Charter network leaders
target_learning_goals: Organizational preparedness, prevention, and response to school decline
examples: Schools that executed replication or expansion before readiness fell into distress; the report recommends readiness checks and leadership support structures before growing a school
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Evan, A., & Sullivan, H. (2021). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 2: The Roles and Perspectives of Charter School Leaders and Board Members. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616211

article_title: State Approaches to Developing Educational Leaders
citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Role-specific professional learning convening role-alike colleagues with applied practice
description: State initiatives frequently provide professional learning designed for particular leadership roles, since "leaders in a particular role may have specific professional learning needs that are not necessarily shared by their colleagues in different roles." These programs bring together role-alike professionals in communities of practice, offer mentorship or coaching, and create opportunities to apply learning at participants' school or district sites. Examples include the Arkansas Leadership Academy's suite of role-differentiated programs (Teacher Leader Program serving 54 participants in 2022–23; Master Principal Program serving 60 across three phases), Delaware's Assistant Principal Academy, and South Carolina's School Leadership Executive Institute serving up to 24 leaders per year.
requirements: Programming must be designed around the substantive distinctions between leadership roles
Programs typically combine role-alike cohorts with mentorship, coaching, or job-embedded application
constraints: The report describes these programs but does not evaluate their quality or outcomes
target_learners: Principals
Assistant principals
Teacher leaders
District administrators
target_learning_goals: Developing role-specific leadership competencies
Connecting with role-alike colleagues
examples: The Arkansas Master Principal Program is a three-phase program over 3 school years in which participants apply learning at their school site, collect evidence of intervention efficacy, and earn the Master Principal designation with bonuses of $25,000 annually for up to 5 years in high-need schools

citation: White, M., Grayson, D., Caparas, R., & Alcalá, L. (2025). Strengthening California's teacher workforce: Toward a statewide strategic framework. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/support/californias-state-educator-workforce-collaborative/

It is accompanied by live career counselors who support prospective teachers in navigating the steps of becoming a teacher. As of March 2025, the report states the Roadmap "had received 123,376 hits and its live career counselors had served nearly 5,000 people," and practitioner testimonials describe it as helping candidates access financial aid information and choose residency pathways.

article_title: Authentic Student Work in College Admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business
citation: Willis, L., & Martinez, M. R. (2022). Authentic student work in college admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/756.774
title: Ross Admissions Portfolio (Business Case Discussion + Artifact)
description: A required student-created portfolio added to the Ross School of Business BBA first-year application in fall 2016. Per the report, "The Ross Admissions Portfolio consists of two components: a Business Case Discussion and an Artifact." The Business Case Discussion is a 500-word essay asking applicants to identify and solve a personally meaningful business-related issue; the Artifact is a 250-word description accompanying multimedia work showing learning applied in or beyond school. Every first-year BBA applicant completes it alongside University of Michigan application materials.
requirements: Aligned to central admission processes without altering University of Michigan deadlines or timelines
Technological capacity (SlideRoom) to accept and transfer multimedia submissions
Rubrics with clear criteria and detailed performance indicators
Trained, calibrated application readers
constraints: Required of all first-year BBA applicants, adding preparation time students estimated at 1 to 2 weeks
Open-ended prompts with no single right way to craft a successful portfolio
target_learners: High school seniors applying to the undergraduate BBA program
target_learning_goals: Demonstrating business mindsets such as problem definition and problem-solving
Demonstrating applied learning and college-success skills such as persistence and collaboration
examples: In the first implementation year the Ross School received nearly 5,000 Artifacts, including documents, images, videos, and audio files

article_title: Bots and Blocks: Presenting a Project-Based Approach for Robotics Education
citation: Tobias Geger, Dominique Briechle and Andreas Rausch. (2026). Bots and Blocks: Presenting a project-based approach for robotics education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14529
title: ROS-based disassembly station with two robots and conveyor belts as the project hardware platform
description: The student project used a hardware disassembly station consisting of two robots and two conveyor belts, with a ROS backbone controlling the robots and adjunct installations. The system exposes topics for moving, rotating, grasping, digital outputs and inputs, joint states, conveyor and clamp control. Because some components were implemented in ROS 1, "a ROS bridge is required in order to integrate all functionalities into the new ROS2 system that the students are implementing." Students aligned the AI camera frame with the world frame via the /tf2 node for precise grasping.
requirements: ROS drivers for both robots and a ROS bridge integrating legacy ROS components into the students' ROS2 system
constraints: Project goal is transferred from complex real products to plastic building bricks (4x2, 2x2 and 2x2 round blocks) configured under rules that keep bricks graspable by the hardware effectors
target_learners: undergraduate student teams working on cyber-physical systems projects
target_learning_goals: robot programming with ROS/ROS2, system integration, and AI-based object detection and localization
examples: Students implemented start and end sequence nodes, integrated component-detection and decision-making nodes, and switched robot control from joint-angle-based to Cartesian coordinate navigation

article_title: Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for AI companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk
citation: Liao, C.-Y. (2026). Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for ai companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-13958-6
title: Role-Adaptive AI Companion Framework: a Modular Adaptive Agent that dynamically switches between Student Peer, Teacher Assistant, and Parent Advisor roles
description: The framework conceptualizes an AI companion as a Modular Adaptive Agent (MAA), inspired by Multi-Agent Systems role-differentiation principles, that "dynamically transitions between three primary roles: the ‘Student Peer’ (facilitating low-stakes dialogue), the ‘Teacher Assistant’ (providing diagnostic analytics), and the ‘Parent Advisor’ (offering actionable home-based guid - ance)." Its core principle is context-aware role adaptability: the agent perceives the user and pedagogical task and modulates its functions, interactional style, and communication register through a modular configuration mechanism, triggered by cues such as user login or task selection. The framework is grounded in scaffolding theory, Learning Companion System principles, and socio-ecological views of family involvement, and its transition logic is justified by the article's empirical competence-gap findings.
requirements: A unified data backbone with Role-Based Access Control and privacy-preserving data protocols so role-appropriate information is shared selectively
Triggers such as user identity or task selection to activate the appropriate role
Access to student interaction data, curriculum data, and student profiles for adaptation
constraints: Conceptualized specifically for elementary reading education and book talk within programs like MSSR
The framework itself was not implemented or evaluated; the empirical study tested only a fixed single-role instantiation
target_learners: Elementary school students in reading programs
Their teachers
Their parents
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and reflective book talk
Factual recall, emotional response, and future-oriented application (4F dimensions)
Teacher instructional decision-making and parental support of reading at home
examples: The formative study instantiated only the Student Peer role using a Whisper-plus-GPT-3.5 conversational system, isolating the single-role baseline the framework is meant to transcend
key_sources: Liao, C.-Y. (2026). Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for ai companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-13958-6

article_title: Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for AI companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk
citation: Liao, C.-Y. (2026). Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for ai companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-13958-6
title: Three role-integration design principles: integrated data governance, context-driven role switching, and synergistic human-AI collaboration
description: The article specifies three paramount design principles for orchestrating multiple AI roles into a cohesive whole. "Permissions and Data Sharing form the ethical backbone of the framework," implemented through Role-Based Access Control so the Teacher Assistant role provides detailed analytics while the Parent Advisor role generates aggregated, non-identifiable summaries. Context-driven adaptability operates on two levels: explicit role switching via pre-defined triggers and implicit stylistic adaptation that recalibrates scaffolding in real time. Synergistic human-AI collaboration requires communication protocols so insights from one role, such as the Student Peer mode, inform another, such as the Teacher Assistant interface.
requirements: Robust Role-Based Access Control and privacy-preserving data protocols compliant with regulations such as GDPR and FERPA
Clear, pre-defined triggers for explicit role switching
Interface loops designed to manage the interplay of roles, users, activities, and data flows
constraints: Stated for the proposed framework's orchestration of roles, not empirically tested in the study
target_learners: Elementary school students
Teachers
Parents
target_learning_goals: Coordinated multi-stakeholder support for reading education and book talk
examples: The Teacher Assistant role exposes configurable analysis parameters and reviewable dashboards, while the Parent Advisor role allows parents to customize information focus to prevent overload

article_title: RoboBuddy in the Classroom: Exploring LLM-Powered Social Robots for Storytelling in Learning and Integration Activities
citation: Tozadore, D., Ertug, N., Chaker, Y., & Abderrahim, M. (2025). RoboBuddy in the Classroom: Exploring LLM-Powered Social Robots for Storytelling in Learning and Integration Activities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16706
title: RoboBuddy teacher interface for generating scenario-based robot activities from curriculum content
description: A browser-based system with three modules: a teacher-facing web interface for preparing storytelling activities, a web application connecting the interface to LLM modules, and a locally runnable fine-tuned LLM so data stays local. Teachers select predefined settings translated into specialized prompts, choose levels of AI assistance (five levels for Story Generation, three for Lecture Storification), specify the age group, and can edit, regenerate, or replace generated stories before approving questions for the robot. Activities run with a virtual avatar or an Alpha Mini robot, with DALL·E-3 image generation whose complexity is tailored to the age group. The article states the goal is to "grant teachers autonomy, using the AI as a supportive tool rather than the primary element in course creation".
requirements: Teachers (or experimenters) prepare activities through the interface and approve generated content before it is sent to the robot
constraints: The local model was chosen for setups with limited computing resources; the article notes concerns about data privacy motivated a local model
target_learners: young primary-school students (average age 6.42) in multicultural classrooms
target_learning_goals: curriculum content approached through scenario-based activities
social integration and inclusion
examples: Over one week, the system supported four co-designed activities: robot-posed questions, student-generated questions, teacher free-style interaction, and the robot composing paragraphs with words from children's primary languages

article_title: Play-Testing REMind: Evaluating an Educational Robot-Mediated Role-Play Game
citation: Elaheh Sanoubari, Neil Fernandes, Keith Rebello, Alicia Pan, Andrew Houston, and Kerstin Dautenhahn. (2026). Play-Testing REMind: Evaluating an Educational Robot-Mediated Role-Play Game. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00300
title: Robot-Mediated Applied Drama (RMAD): robots as embodied dramatic proxies for social-emotional learning
description: Robot-Mediated Applied Drama is a pedagogical framework in which social robots are used "not as tutors, but as embodied dramatic proxies" through which learners simulate social situations, reflect on emotional nuances, and rehearse prosocial action. Drawing on Forum Theatre, a Joker facilitator guides reflection while a Wizard orchestrates the drama. The article positions RMAD as a promising framework for supporting anti-bullying social-emotional learning by combining embodiment, narrative, and rehearsal.

Embodied robot characters that enact the social scenario and respond to the learner's rehearsed intervention
constraints: The article reports only an early-stage evaluation of a complex, semi-autonomous research prototype; durable behavioral change was not tested
target_learners: children aged 9-10 in anti-bullying education
target_learning_goals: social-emotional learning, including empathy, perspective-taking, and bystander intervention
examples: REMind instantiates RMAD with three Furhat robots playing the avatar, victim, and bully in a five-phase interactive narrative

article_title: RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming With Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking
citation: Leyi Li, Chenyu Du, Jiafei Sun, Erick Purwanto, and Qing Zhang. (2026). RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming with Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking. Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813071
title: RoboBlockly Studio: integrated block-based programming, conversational AI teaching agent, and embodied robot execution
description: RoboBlockly Studio is a web-based framework integrating "block-based visual programming, conversational AI, and robot embodiment to enhance the development of computational thinking skills". The backend converts visual code to Python and transmits it via WebSocket to a Mecanum-wheeled robot with a multi-joint arm running ROS 2 on a Jetson Orin Nano. The AI agent (GPT-4o via OpenAI API, temperature 0, not fine-tuned) checks tasks, produces block-grounded feedback, and provides hints, with prompts encoding task rules and a rolling 20-message interaction history including the workspace XML.
requirements: Task-specific prompts that explicitly encode the relevant rules, constraints, and success criteria for each task to reduce unconstrained model judgment
constraints: During program execution, the robot cannot be interrupted or controlled; learners observe, consult the AI, and revise through subsequent runs
target_learners: high school students with no prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: computational thinking: decomposition, abstraction, algorithms, debugging
examples: Students author programs in a dual-panel interface, submit them via a chat bubble with a Run the Robot button, and observe execution on a 5×5 grid mat with obstacles and manipulable cubes

title: Mapping robot types onto 4E cognition dimensions and competence domains

article_title: The effects of educational robotics in STEM education: a multilevel meta-analysis
citation: Fan Ouyang and Weiqi Xu. (2024). The effects of educational robotics in STEM education: a multilevel meta-analysis. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-024-00469-4
title: Robot-assisted STEM education as a complex system of interacting elements
description: The article frames robot-assisted STEM education as a complex system arising from interactions among multiple elements beyond the technology itself. It states that robot-assisted STEM education "can be viewed as a complex system that arises from the interactions between technologies (i.e., educational robotics), human subjects (e.g., instructors, students), information (e.g., discipline knowledge), mediums (e.g., interactive types), and external environment (e.g., intervention durations)". This holistic framing motivates the coding of eight moderator variables (discipline, educational level, instructor support, instructional strategy, interactive type, intervention duration, robotic type, control group condition) in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Analysis of robotics effects must consider technological, human, informational, medium, and environmental elements together rather than the technology alone
constraints: The framework is theoretical; the meta-analysis found only discipline significantly moderated effects empirically
target_learners: K-16 students in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding conditions under which educational robotics improves STEM learning
examples: The authors coded eight moderator variables spanning technology, human, information, medium, and environment elements across the 21 included studies

title: RoundTable written turn-taking structure
description: RoundTable (Kagan, 1994) is a cooperative method in which the teacher organizes heterogeneous groups of three or four, gives each group a pen and sheet of paper, and presents a task requiring more than one answer. The article says it helps students solve complex conceptual problems, developing analysis, synthesis, and evaluation skills.

A task requiring more than one answer
Stipulated time for completion and per-member writing

target_learning_goals: Analysis, synthesis, and evaluation skills
Reviewing peers' written work and considering other points of view
examples: Students reviewed work written by peers, which the article says develops conceptual understanding and the ability to evaluate information

citation: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 365–370. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9204-9

citation: Maëlle Neveu, Marie Geurten, Nancy Durieux, Laurence Rousselle. (2023). Finger Use and Arithmetic Skills in Children and Adolescents: a Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09722-8
title: Roesch and Moeller's three-stage developmental model of fingers' contribution to numerical development
description: The review presents a developmental model proposed by Roesch and Moeller (2015) that assigns fingers a changing role across three stages of numerical development. At the first stage, when children learn the number-word sequence, "fingers support the segmentation of this sequence by the association of each raised finger with a specific number word," and procedural counting with fingers supports early conceptual knowledge such as cardinality. At the second stage, number gestures communicate the cardinal of a set and support learning cardinal values of new number words. At the third stage, when children start to calculate, they "mobilizing fingers as an external support" while drawing on counting and cardinal skills. The review uses this model to frame why the role of fingers may differ across numerical tasks and developmental stages.
requirements: Children progress through stages of learning the number-word sequence, the cardinal principle, and initial calculation, with fingers serving a different function at each stage.
constraints: The model was proposed to clarify fingers' contribution across numerical development generally; the review notes the benefit of finger use is mainly debated specifically for arithmetic development.
target_learners: Children from preschool through primary school learning number words, cardinality, and early arithmetic
target_learning_goals: Number-word sequence learning
Cardinality understanding
Early arithmetic calculation skills
examples: The review cites finger counting supporting segmentation of the number-word sequence, tagging items during procedural counting, communicating set cardinality, and serving as external support during early calculation.

title: RoSTraC cloud-based learning platform for self-contained training
description: The RoSTraC cloud is an interactive file-hosting platform (Google Drive and iCloud) through which "The cloud provides access to theoretical basics of RAS, instructions, and video tutorials of the RoSTraC exercises." Trainees upload learning progress for documentation and assessment, and trainee-created video lectures are added interactively. Regular video meetings complement the platform for sharing progress and analyzing procedure videos. It enables self-contained training at the trainee's own institution without traveling or permanent supervision.

title: Rosenberg self-esteem scale and 26-item self-esteem-related behavior questionnaire with pilot reliability
description: The study instrument combined demographic items, Rosenberg's 10-item self-esteem scale on a 4-point Likert scale, and a researcher-developed 26-item behavior questionnaire. In a pilot with 39 participants, the Rosenberg scale showed "a reliability result of 0.777 Cronbach Alpha", the behavior questionnaire 0.905, and the overall reliability 0.841, which the authors took as indicating the questionnaires were valid for use.

constraints: The authors state the behavioral questionnaire was researcher-developed and not a well-established, standardized questionnaire

target_learning_goals: measuring self-esteem and self-esteem-related behaviors in medical students
examples: Distributed electronically via social media platforms to medical students across 5 regions of Saudi Arabia from March to December 2022

article_title: The Effect on Performance Time and Quality of the Knots after Mono or Bimanual Training of Laparoscopic Intracorporeal Knot Tying according to the Gladiator Rule Technique.
citation: Asencio FA, Ribeiro HASA, Romeo A, Wattiez A, Ribeiro PAGA. (2018). The Effect on Performance Time and Quality of the Knots after Mono or Bimanual Training of Laparoscopic Intracorporeal Knot Tying according to the Gladiator Rule Technique. Rev Bras Ginecol Obstet. https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0038-1649494
title: Romeo Gladiator Rule two-day laparoscopic suturing training course with pelvic trainer
description: A two-day laparoscopic suture training course built around the Romeo Gladiator Rule knot-tying technique, in which "the needle holder performs a clockwise turn (from 6 to 12 o'clock) or a counterclockwise turn (from 12 to 6 o'clock) with the jaws of the tip open" to keep the thread in place. The course combines 5 hours 30 minutes of theory (ergonomics, energy, suture) with 8 hours 30 minutes of hands-on practice in a pelvic trainer simulator, three residents per supervised workstation, using landmarks called the home base and the thread horizon. The study used it to compare monomanual versus bimanual knot-tying training.
requirements: Resident participants without prior laparoscopic suture training, working in groups of 3 per supervised workstation with a tutor
A pelvic trainer with all-in-one laparoscopic video system, 10-mm 0-degree optics, and two 5-mm lateral trocars with needle holders
constraints: The authors state the data reflect specifically the studied population in a specific condition of knowledge and training, and that clinical practice with living tissue was not tested
target_learners: second- and third-year gynecology/obstetrics and general surgery residents without prior laparoscopic suture training
target_learning_goals: intracorporeal laparoscopic knot tying
laparoscopic suturing skill and knot quality
examples: Group A trained with the dominant hand only; group B trained with both hands, each following its own blocking sequence for the complete intracorporeal knot

article_title: Procedural virtual reality simulation training for robotic surgery: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Raison Nicholas, Harrison Patrick, Abe Takashige, Aydin Abdullatif, Ahmed Kamran, Dasgupta Prokar. (2021). Procedural virtual reality simulation training for robotic surgery: a randomised controlled trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-020-08197-w
title: RobotiX Mentor robot-assisted radical prostatectomy (RARP) guided procedural VR module
description: The RobotiX Mentor (3D Systems) is a robotic surgery VR simulator whose RARP module provides guided, step-by-step procedural training. The article states that "The module consists of four training tasks; bladder neck dissection (BND), neurovascular bundle dissection, apical dissection and urethrovesical anastomosis (UVA)", of which BND and UVA were used for training in this trial. Successful completion of modules was determined by competency scores provided by the simulator software.
requirements: Guided training modules with step-by-step procedural guidance were used throughout the study
Competency scores provided by the RobotiX Mentor software determined successful completion of each module
constraints: The neurovascular bundle and apical dissection tasks were excluded because they require specialist anatomical knowledge for successful completion
target_learners: Novice medical students with no experience in robotic surgery
target_learning_goals: Robotic surgical technical skills including endowrist manipulation, camera navigation, dissection and diathermy use
examples: The procedural VR cohort trained over 5 weeks in 1-h sessions using the guided BND and UVA tasks with ad hoc guidance from an expert robotic surgeon

article_title: Medical student experience with robot-assisted surgery after limited laparoscopy exposure.
citation: Nasit V, Vongsurbchart T, Myszka A, Richter P, Rogula T. (2021). Medical student experience with robot-assisted surgery after limited laparoscopy exposure. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-020-01129-9
title: Train robotic surgery skills in a robot-assisted simulation environment rather than relying on laparoscopy exposure
description: The authors conclude that because limited laparoscopy training did not change initial robotic performance, "training in robotic surgery ought to take place in a robot-assisted simulation environment." They note validated robotic curricula such as the Fundamentals of Robotic Surgery offer novices a direct path without an intermediate laparoscopy step.
requirements: Access to a robot-assisted simulation environment or validated robotic surgery curriculum such as the Fundamentals of Robotic Surgery
constraints: Simulators are not yet available for the Senhance Surgical System, per the article
target_learners: novice medical students and surgery trainees without prior robotic experience
target_learning_goals: fundamental robotic psychomotor skills such as depth perception, bimanual coordination, and instrument clutching
examples: In the study, 0, 20, and 40 min laparoscopy training groups showed no significant objective or subjective differences on robotic tasks, motivating the recommendation

article_title: A review of simulation training and new 3D computer-generated synthetic organs for robotic surgery education.
citation: Costello Daniel M., Huntington Isabel, Burke Grace, Farrugia Brooke, O'Connor Andrea J., Costello Anthony J., Thomas Benjamin C., Dundee Philip, Ghazi Ahmed, Corcoran Niall. (2021). A review of simulation training and new 3D computer-generated synthetic organs for robotic surgery education. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-021-01302-8
title: University of Rochester 3D-printed PVA-hydrogel synthetic organ model platform for robotic surgical simulation
description: The Rochester Simulation Innovation Laboratory produces "computer-generated printed organ models using printed moulds and polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) hydrogel" for validated robotic simulation of kidney transplant, partial nephrectomy, radical prostatectomy and penile implant surgery. Models are cast from 3D-printed injection moulds generated from patient MRI segmentations, frozen–thawed to tune tissue stiffness, and perfused with simulated blood flow, cautery and suturability properties. Embedded nerve strain and energy gauges capture clinically relevant performance metrics such as nerve tension, positive margins, anastomotic leak, blood loss and operating time.
requirements: Access to patient imaging (e.g., MRI) for segmentation, a 3D printer, injection moulds and PVA hydrogel processing including freeze-thaw cycles
constraints: Commercially available synthetic models are not cost-effective and have not been academically validated
The current cost of equipment, slow fabrication time and small-scale production limit widespread adoption
The validity of Saba et al.'s kidney transplant model was limited to a single surgeon single centre study
target_learners: surgical trainees and residents in robotic surgery (urology, gynaecology, general and colorectal surgery)
target_learning_goals: robotic surgical procedural skills and competency prior to live surgery
examples: Ghazi et al.'s 2020 partial nephrectomy model validated with 43 participants; Witthaus et al.'s prostatectomy model with embedded nerve strain gauges on which experts produced 0% positive margins versus 77.8% of novices

citation: McWilliam R. A., Boavida Tânia, Bull Kerry, Cañadas Margarita, Hwang Ai-Wen, Józefacka Natalia, Lim Hong Huay, Pedernera Marisú, Sergnese Tamara, Woodward Julia. (2020). The Routines-Based Model Internationally Implemented. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17228308
title: The Routines-Based Model: needs assessment and intervention planning, a consultative approach, and a method for running classrooms
description: The Routines-Based Model (RBM) is an early intervention framework with three main components: "needs assessment and intervention planning, a consultative approach, and a method for running classrooms." It "focuses on children's functioning in everyday routines and on family needs, strengths, and capacities." Its hallmark practices are the Routines-Based Interview, support-based visits with families, and a focus on child engagement. The article reports the model is implemented in 10 countries and that implementers valued it because it "provides actual practices for implementing a family-centered approach."
requirements: A list of goals meaningful to the family and other caregivers, developed through an ecomap and a Routines-Based Interview
constraints: The whole model is not implemented by any one program; adopters select components
target_learners: Young children with disabilities (birth–6 years) and their families in early intervention
target_learning_goals: Child functioning and participation in everyday routines
Family capacity-building and confidence
examples: Noah's Ark in Australia implemented the RBI with 150 staff working with over 2000 families after a 4 day boot camp trained 18 additional trainers

article_title: Factors predicting students' performance in the final pediatrics OSCE.
citation: Al Rushood Maysoun, Al-Eisa Amal. (2020). Factors predicting students’ performance in the final pediatrics OSCE. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0236484
title: Distribute student rotations across the year according to training-center capacity without expecting harm to final OSCE performance
description: From the finding that clerkship timing showed no consistent effect on final OSCE performance, the authors recommend: "dividing students to complete different rotations throughout the year, according to the capacity of the training centers, staff availability, and applied curriculum, should not affect their performance on final exams". They attribute this to students' good long-term clinical capacities.
requirements: A final examination common to all rotation groups and rotation slots filled across the academic year
constraints: The one significant pooled pairwise difference (third vs second rotation, P = 0.029) was not present in individual years; middle-of-year rotations were interrupted by many holidays
target_learners: 6th-year clinical medical students
target_learning_goals: Retention and later application of clinical skills learned during rotations
examples: Students were divided into three groups rotating through pediatrics, obstetrics-gynecology and other subspecialties across the year, and final OSCE means by rotation slot differed only for third vs second in the pooled sample

article_title: Listen to the outpatient: qualitative explanatory study on medical students' recognition of outpatients' narratives in combined ambulatory clerkship and peer role-play.
citation: Takahashi Noriyuki, Aomatsu Muneyoshi, Saiki Takuya, Otani Takashi, Ban Nobutaro. (2018). Listen to the outpatient: qualitative explanatory study on medical students' recognition of outpatients' narratives in combined ambulatory clerkship and peer role-play. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1336-6
title: Combine ambulatory clerkship with peer role-play so students can reflect on outpatients' perspectives
description: The article argues for pairing clerkship encounters with role-play because reflection is otherwise rare: "it is often difficult for medical students to reflect on their patients because of limitations in time, space, and teaching staff." The role-play exercise "allowed students to attend to patients' narratives", and role-play fosters reflection of patients' perspectives in undergraduate medical education.
requirements: Real outpatient encounters during the clerkship whose narratives can be re-enacted
A facilitated role-play and group discussion session after the encounter
constraints: The research does not suggest that peer role-play is necessary to learn patients' narratives
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in ambulatory clerkships
target_learning_goals: reflecting on patients' perspectives and attending to patients' narratives
examples: Students acted as the outpatients they had interviewed, then watched the role-play video and discussed communication skills, clinical reasoning, and the information the patient actually gave
